newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec had separation fund says former premier.
newsitem.headline: Quebec had separation fund says former premier.

text.p: Quebec had set aside a secret C$19 billion fund to smooth the way to independence if the Canadian province had voted to separate in October 1995, former Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau said on Monday.

In an interview broadcast on the French-language TVA television network late Monday night, Parizeau confirmed that his separatist Parti Quebecois government had arranged the secret fund to help weather any economic crisis provoked by a vote for Quebec sovereignty.
"Almost anything could have happened on the financial markets. We were quite ready," Parizeau said.

Parizeau said C$19 billion was held by a "triangle of financial protection", comprising the Quebec government's department of finance, the government-owned electrical utility Hydro-Quebec, and the Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec, which manages C$51 billion of public pension and insurance fund assets.
Separatists lost the October 30, 1995, referendum on Quebec sovereignty by 1.2 percentage points. Parizeau resigned as premier the next day.

In the TVA interview, Parizeau also indicated that he was prepared to move quickly to make Quebec sovereign, even though separatists had promised they would hold one year of negotiations with Canada on creating a new economic or even political partnership.
Parizeau said he had taken steps to garner a quick recognition from France of a referendum vote for Quebec sovereignty.
"There absolutely had to be a rapid recognition," Parizeau said.
Parizeau said quick recognition from France would have prodded the United States into also recognizing a democratic vote for Quebec independence.

"Basically, through the French we were aiming at the Americans. It was absolutely necessary that the Americans, how do I say it, be more or less in the atmosphere of business of usual. And for that, someone had to push them in the back, and that (was) the role of the French," Parizeau said.
Parizeau said he had expected swift recognition from France because that country's National Assembly was in session at the time of the referendum.
